physics-killer-03.title: A $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ object slides
physics-killer-03.goal: Apply principles to solve the inquiry problem.
physics-killer-03.material: A $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ object slides from rest from a height of $4\,\mathrm{m}$ down a frictionless curved surface, crosses a rough horizontal section of length $5\,\mathrm{m}$ (constant friction force of magnitude $11\,\mathrm{N}$ on the object), and then climbs a frictionless incline on the right. Use $g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and ignore air resistance. Which option correctly gives, in order, the thermal energy $Q$ produced in the rough section and the maximum height reached on the right incline?
physics-killer-03.s.s1.prompt: A $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ object slides from rest from a height of $4\,\mathrm{m}$ down a frictionless curved surface, crosses a rough horizontal section of length $5\,\mathrm{m}$ (constant friction force of magnitude $11\,\mathrm{N}$ on the object), and then climbs a frictionless incline on the right. Use $g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and ignore air resistance. Which option correctly gives, in order, the thermal energy $Q$ produced in the rough section and the maximum height reached on the right incline?
physics-killer-03.s.s1.explain: Initial mechanical energy $E_0=mgh_0=2\cdot10\cdot4=80\,\mathrm{J}$. In the rough section $Q=fs=11\cdot5=55\,\mathrm{J}$ becomes heat, so $80-55=25\,\mathrm{J}$ of mechanical energy remains. The right incline is frictionless, so $25=mgh$ gives $h=\dfrac{25}{2\cdot10}=1.25\,\mathrm{m}$. Assuming the object returns to $4\,\mathrm{m}$ ignores friction (option 2); mistaking the remaining $25\,\mathrm{J}$ for the heat gives option 3; using $\frac12mgh$ instead of $mgh$ gives $2.5\,\mathrm{m}$ (option 4).
physics-killer-03.s.s2.prompt: Which scenario demonstrates the correct real-world application of this principle?
physics-killer-03.s.s2.explain: The fundamental principles of this inquiry are widely implemented in modern technology.
